clue.text: Slides and photographs taken for talk

indicators.note: something offered for talk is spoken, so the word is wanted by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: photo shoots are sessions where photographs are taken

explanation.surface: Someone prepares a talk with slides and photographs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slides' looks like projector slides to go with the photographs, but it means playground slides.
explanation.definitionFit: Chutes are sloping channels down which people or goods slide, as in a water park.

clue.text: Low sound and soft to carry with difficulty

blocks.note: a low continuous drone
p is piano, the musical marking for soft

explanation.surface: Someone groans quietly while lugging something heavy.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, to hump a load is to heave or lug it with effort, usually on the back.

clue.text: Cut right at end, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the words that come before are only one possible arrangement of their letters

blocks.note: taken as written
the usual abbreviation
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something trimmed squarely at its tail end.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the letters to rearrange and a description of the result: something truncated may well be cut right at its end.
explanation.definitionFit: Truncated means shortened by having a part, especially the end, lopped off.

clue.text: Drink to keep girl on the right lines

blocks.note: the pronoun for a girl
the usual abbreviation
railway lines, abbreviated RY

explanation.surface: A drink meant to keep a girl behaving properly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the right lines' reads as an idiom for behaving well, but it splits into right and lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherry is a fortified wine from southern Spain, served as an aperitif.

clue.text: Buffer state head meets East European

indicators.note: meets says one piece comes up against the other, so they are set side by side

blocks.note: from Poland, in eastern Europe
ER, Elizabeth Regina, the Queen as head of state

explanation.surface: A buffer state's leader holds talks with an Eastern European.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buffer state' is a political phrase, but 'Buffer' alone is the definition and 'state head' is the Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: A buffer is a pad or tool for shining a surface, which is what a polisher does.

clue.text: Find touch

blocks.note: first meaning: to identify or pin down exactly
second meaning: literally to place a digit on something

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, each a meaning of the same phrase: one figurative, one literal.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to identify something precisely, and taken literally it means to touch with a digit.

clue.text: Slurred song, gathered round musical instrument

indicators.note: something gathered round another object encloses it, so one word wraps around the other

blocks.note: a lied is a German art song
a bell is a percussion instrument

explanation.surface: Singers slurring their song as they gather round an instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slurred' suggests sloppy singing, but here it means smeared someone's name.
explanation.definitionFit: To slur someone is to make damaging insinuations about them, and to libel is to defame them in print.

clue.text: Son to Holy Joe is a rare youth

blocks.note: the usual abbreviation
a Holy Joe is a sanctimonious, self-righteous person

explanation.surface: A pious man's son turns out to be a remarkable youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rare' flags that this sense is now uncommon. Holy Joe is an informal British term for a sanctimonious person.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprig is a dated, uncommon word for a young man or lad, an offshoot of a family.

clue.text: Horseman breaking a rein, out of the hunt

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it, so one piece sits within the other
out means disordered or not in place, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a quest is a search or hunt

explanation.surface: A rider breaks a rein and drops out of the fox hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: An equestrian is a rider of horses, especially a skilled one.

clue.text: Current member's snobbish, hollow and cocky

blocks.note: I is the physics symbol for electric current
Member of Parliament
U means upper-class, as in U and non-U usage
a dent is a hollow in a surface

explanation.surface: A sitting MP who is snobbish, empty and arrogant.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from the 1950s 'U and non-U' classification of British speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Impudent means cheeky and disrespectful, much like being brash or cocky.

clue.text: Sailing ship makes bay from the sound

indicators.note: judging from the sound means going by how the word is said, not spelt

blocks.note: a dog's bay is its bark

explanation.surface: A sailing ship comes into a bay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bay' suggests a coastal inlet beside the ship, but it is the cry of a hound.
explanation.definitionFit: A barque is a sailing vessel with three or more masts, square-rigged except at the stern.

clue.text: One has placed an order for The Times

definitions.text: One has placed an order for The Times

blocks.clueFragment: One has placed an order for The Times
blocks.note: surface reading: a customer ordering the newspaper from a newsagent
setter's reading: someone who puts dates and periods into sequence

explanation.walkthrough: The capitalised newspaper title is a decoy; 'times' simply means periods of history, and 'order' means sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: This specialist arranges events and dates into their correct historical sequence.

clue.text: Made to hold in one's wind, perhaps

definitions.text: Made to hold in one's wind, perhaps

blocks.clueFragment: Made to hold in one's wind
blocks.note: surface reading: someone forced to hold their breath or suppress flatulence
setter's reading: an object designed to be filled with air, like a lilo or dinghy

explanation.walkthrough: 'One's wind' sounds bodily, but the wind is simply air pumped into a rubber object.
explanation.definitionFit: An airbed or rubber dinghy is designed to be blown up and to stay filled with air.

clue.text: Bow taken by little bird?

blocks.note: first meaning: a tied loop of ribbon or string
second meaning: a small wading sandpiper

explanation.surface: A tiny bird makes a curtsey.
explanation.definitionFit: A bow is a decorative tie fastening, and the same word names a stocky shorebird of the sandpiper family.

clue.text: Rings for ties, American style

blocks.note: first meaning: small hoop earrings worn to keep a piercing open
second meaning: Americans call railway ... ties

explanation.surface: Swapping jewellery for neckties the way Americans do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ties' are not neckties but the beams under railway track, which the British call by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: These are both plain hoop earrings and the wooden or concrete beams that support railway track.

clue.text: Father in tears at time of birth

blocks.note: informal word for a father
a rent is a rip or tear
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A father weeping at the moment his child is born.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tears' reads as crying, but it means rips.
explanation.definitionFit: Birth in the sense of lineage or origin: one's parentage is one's descent.

clue.text: Bully leading batting order in game

indicators.note: leading means going in front, so the first piece is placed before the next
in says the joined pieces sit inside the following word

blocks.note: the Order of Merit, a British honour
a batsman in cricket is in
deer are hunted as game

explanation.surface: A bully insists on opening the batting order in a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batting order' reads as a cricket line-up, but it splits: 'order' is the Order of Merit and 'game' is hunted animals.
explanation.definitionFit: To bully is to throw one's weight around and intimidate, which is to domineer over others.

clue.text: Pleased to have one of these flowers, in short

blocks.clueFragment: Pleased to have one of these flowers
blocks.note: surface reading: someone delighted to be given a bloom
setter's reading: the word for pleased is also the short name for one of these flowers

explanation.walkthrough: Gardeners shorten the singular of this flower to 'glad', which also means pleased, so 'Pleased' is one of them in short.
explanation.definitionFit: These are sword-leaved plants with tall spikes of bright blooms, often grown for cutting.

clue.text: Animal producing beef, good cut

indicators.note: cut means removed, so the named letter is taken out

blocks.note: to beef is to complain or grumble
the usual abbreviation

explanation.surface: A farm animal yields a good cut of beef.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beef' and 'cut' suggest butchery, but beef is a complaint and cut removes a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A roan is a horse or cow whose coat has white hairs mixed through a darker colour.

clue.text: Dish in lively nightclub is heartless

indicators.note: without a heart means the centre letter is removed

blocks.note: a hot spot is a busy, fashionable nightspot

explanation.surface: A meal served in a fashionable club that has no soul.
explanation.walkthrough: Hotpot, as in Lancashire hotpot, is a lamb and potato stew baked under sliced potatoes.
explanation.definitionFit: Hotpot is a slow-baked casserole of meat and vegetables, a dish served at the table.

clue.text: Resigning, reputation having fallen

blocks.note: one's standing is one's status or repute
something fallen is down

explanation.surface: An official quits after their reputation has collapsed.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand down is to withdraw from an office or post, which is what someone quitting does.

clue.text: Lake's former name is name taken by a state on the up

indicators.note: taken by means picked up after, so this piece follows the others
in a down entry going up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
to state is to say
the usual abbreviation

explanation.surface: A lake's old name has been adopted by a rising nation.
explanation.walkthrough: Lake Malawi in Africa was formerly known as Lake Nyasa, under British colonial rule.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the colonial-era name of the great African lake now called Malawi.

clue.text: Take a dim view of mole's noise

indicators.note: a noise is a sound, so the word wanted is one that is pronounced the same

blocks.note: a mole is a stone breakwater or jetty

explanation.surface: Disapproving of the sound a burrowing mole makes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mole' suggests the burrowing animal, but it is a harbour wall. 'Take a dim view' is literal: look hard in poor light.
explanation.definitionFit: To peer is to look closely with screwed-up eyes, as when straining to see in poor visibility.

clue.text: Monastic, or of this world?

definitions.note: the answer is usually a noun, a person attached to a monastery

blocks.note: first meaning: a lay person dedicated to a religious order
second meaning: describing the flattened spheroid shape of the Earth

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone is otherworldly and cloistered or worldly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of this world' sounds like worldly, the opposite of monastic, but it describes Earth's geometric figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a person is dedicated to a monastery, and the Earth is a sphere flattened at the poles.

clue.text: Gun to make soldiers safe, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard or said, so the wanted word is spelt differently from the one named

blocks.note: the Royal Engineers
peter is old criminal slang for a safe

explanation.surface: A gun to keep troops out of harm's way, so it is said.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Safe' looks like an adjective meaning unharmed, but it is a strongbox, which safecrackers called a peter.
explanation.definitionFit: A repeater is a firearm that fires several shots without reloading.

clue.text: Accelerator can noisily exceed 100 mph? About right!

indicators.note: noisily means out loud, so the phrase is wanted as spoken, not spelt
about means surrounding, so the other letters wrap around this one

blocks.note: a ton is a hundred miles an hour, so to exceed it is to beat a ton
the usual abbreviation

explanation.surface: Asking whether a car's accelerator can push it past 100 mph, then confirming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Accelerator' suggests a car pedal, but it is a physics machine. 'Ton' as 100 mph is British biker slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A betatron is a particle accelerator that speeds up electrons in a circular magnetic field.

clue.text: That lot banked gold, the result of speculation

indicators.note: money banked is held inside an account, so one word is kept within the other

blocks.note: that lot means those people
or is the heraldic term for gold

explanation.surface: A group invested their gold after speculating on the market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speculation' suggests financial gambling, but it means conjecture.
explanation.definitionFit: A theory is an idea formed by reasoning and conjecture rather than proven fact.
